newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Shots fired on Korean border before Cohen visit.
newsitem.headline: Shots fired on Korean border before Cohen visit.

text.p: North and South Korean troops exchanged warning shots at their tense border on Thursday, shortly before U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen visited the area, a Seoul military spokesman said.
Southern troops on patrol within the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) fired 10 warning shots after spotting a group of North Korean soldiers who had crossed the border line, the spokesman said.
"The North Korean soldiers fired back warning shots and withdrew," he said.
The shooting in the eastern sector of the heavily-fortified DMZ took place at 9.30 a.m. (0030 GMT).
Cohen flew by helicopter to the border village of Panmnmunjom, about 100 km (60 miles) west of the flashpoint, after leaving the South Korean defence ministry at 10 a.m., the spokesman said.
The DMZ, set up as a buffer zone under a truce agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War, is just a few minutes flying time from the capital.
South Korean troops broadcast warnings through loudspeakers at five or six North Koreans near the Military Demarcation Line before firing shots into the air, the spokesman said.
The demarcation line runs through the middle of the four-km (2.5 mile)-wide DMZ.
"There have been exchanges of fire in the past, but this was the first shooting incident at the border this year," the spokesman said.
There have been numerous violent border incidents over the past four decades along what is now the world's last Cold War-era frontier.
The most grisly episode occurred in 1976, when North Korean soldiers axed to death two U.S. military officers pruning an overgrown tree in Panmunjom.
Cohen, standing at the border, denounced North Korea's "decaying and dying" communist system and called on Pyongyang to make peace with South Korea.
Earlier, Pyongyang had slammed Cohen for remarks he had made about troop deployments on the Korean peninsula.
"They remain perhaps one of the few countries in the world today that still subscribe to a communist theology and economic system, which is decaying and dying," Cohen told reporters.
The secretary, winding up his first visit to the western Pacific and Asia, was asked if he had a message for the leadership of North Korea, which is on the brink of famine.

"If they can read my lips, I would hope that they would see the futility of putting up signs and trying to promote propaganda of a failed and failing system," he said, while being closely watched by North Korean border guards.
Cohen said he hoped North Korea would recognise "sooner rather than later" the benefits of South Korea's democracy.

"But in the meantime, we have to remain ever vigilant... at a time when it seems to me that their economy and their entire system needs some relief from the burden that they have been carrying for too many years," he said.

Pyongyang's state radio attacked comments by Cohen that virtually all 37,000 troops the United States has in South Korea would remain for the forseeable future, even if the Koreas made peace and were united.

"This outrageous comment puts military pressure on us and reveals the U.S. military forces' dangerous ambition for domination of the entire Korean peninusla," the radio said in a broadcast monitored in Tokyo.
Cohen flew to Panmunjom after talks with South Korean defence minister Kim Dong-jin on how to respond to a new menace posed by North Korea's chroni food shortage.

Cohen and Kim "shared the opinion that military threats from North Korea continued and that a policy of deterrence is most urgently needed in view of uncertainty of North Korea's future", a Seoul defence ministry statement said.
They also "agreed on the need to maintain war preparedness of the combined U.S.-South Korean forces".
"Both sides will make common efforts to effectively deal with any unstable situation in North Korea," the statement added.
